After ai the visarga (as रु) is sounded r before the voiced n.

samasa.sense: the love owed to a father — the sons’ love for him
samasa.alt: Also read as a saptamī tatpuruṣa, पितरि स्नेहः ‘love toward the father’; the sense is the same. Read as ‘a father’s love (for his sons)’ it would not fit: the sons are the ones who cast it off.
Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, धनस्य लुब्धाः; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Present of √कृ (stem करो- before the first-person ending -मि). In a question the present is deliberative: ‘what am I to do?’
Absolutive with ल्यप् (-य), the form used when the verb has a prefix (contrast त्यक्त्वा). Its subject is the agent of the main verb, here the kin (यैः).
Abstract noun in -ता (taddhita तल्) from निष्ठुर ‘hard’. मनः निष्ठुरतां न बध्नाति: ‘the mind does not take on hardness’ — the merchant cannot make himself stop caring.

mantras.anvaya: किं करोमि? मम मनः निष्ठुरतां न बध्नाति। यैः धनलुब्धैः पितृस्नेहं संत्यज्य (अहं) निराकृतः, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A question, then a statement; the second line opens a relative clause (यैः … निराकृतः) whose correlative तेषु and main clause come in 1.32.
mantras.lit: What am I to do? My mind does not take on hardness. Those greedy for wealth by whom, having cast off love for a father, I was spurned —
mantras.tr: What can I do? My heart will not grow hard. Those who, greedy for my wealth, threw off the love they owed their father and drove me out —
mantras.tr_note: ‘my’ with wealth and ‘their’ with father are supplied from the context; the sentence continues in 1.32.

comm.t: The merchant answers with a helpless question. He knows how he was treated and cannot stop loving: his mind refuses the hardness that reason would justify.

The verb बन्ध् ‘to bind’ is the word the text will use for saṃsāra itself (संसारबन्ध, 1.58). Here it is turned around: the mind will not bind itself to hardness, because it is already bound by affection.

samasa.vigraha: पतिश्च स्वजनश्च पतिस्वजनौ; पतिस्वजनयोः हार्दम्, तत्
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (objective genitive) containing an itaretara dvandva (पतिस्वजन)
samasa.literal: affection of (= toward) husband and kinsman
samasa.sense: the love a wife owes her husband and kin owe a kinsman — which they too threw off
samasa.alt: स्वजन is itself a karmadhāraya, स्वः जनः ‘one’s own person, a kinsman’. The dvandva may also be taken as plural (पतिस्वजनाः).

samasa.sense: a respectful address to the king

morph.note: Neuter nominative of हार्दिन् ‘having हार्द (affection)’, agreeing with मनः. The masculine nominative of the same word, हार्दी, comes in 1.43.
Present participle of √ज्ञा (stem जानत्), nominative singular masculine. With अपि it is concessive: ‘though knowing’.
The prefix अभि sharpens ‘know’ to ‘understand, recognise’: the merchant knows the facts (जानन्) but cannot see into them (न अभिजानामि).

mantras.anvaya: (यैः) पतिस्वजनहार्दं च (संत्यज्य अहं निराकृतः), तेषु एव मे मनः हार्दि (अस्ति)। महामते, जानन् अपि एतत् किं (इति) न अभिजानामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first half closes the relative sentence of 1.31: पतिस्वजनहार्दम् is a second object of संत्यज्य, and तेषु … हार्दि is the main clause. The second half is a new sentence: an indirect question (किम् एतत्) governed by न अभिजानामि.
mantras.lit: — and affection for husband and kinsman: toward those very ones my mind is loving. What this is I do not understand, though knowing, O great-minded one.
mantras.tr: who threw off all feeling for husband and kinsman — toward them, still, my heart is full of love. I know all this, wise king, and yet I cannot understand it.

comm.t: The merchant states the paradox the sage will be asked to explain: he knows (जानन्) and yet does not understand (न अभिजानामि). The facts are clear to him; his heart does not follow them.
This is the condition Medhas will name in 1.55: Mahāmāyā draws away the minds even of those who know (ज्ञानिनामपि चेतांसि). Knowledge of the facts is not freedom from delusion.
A modern reading: the text separates information from understanding. The merchant is not ignorant; he is attached — and he is honest enough to say that the two are different.

samasa.alt: Also read as a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa, प्रेम्णा प्रवणम् ‘bent by love’; the sense is close. प्रेमन् drops its final n as the first member of a compound.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (prādi: the prefix वि stands for विगत)
samasa.sense: worthless, who have behaved without virtue

morph.note: Present of √जन् in the fourth class (stem जाय-), ātmanepada. It is singular with two subjects joined by च (निःश्वासः, दौर्मनस्यम्), agreeing with the nearer or taking the pair as one experience.
Abstract noun with vṛddhi of the first syllable (taddhita ष्यञ्): दुर्मनस् ‘ill-minded, dejected’ → दौर्मनस्य ‘dejection’.
Locative of कृत ‘done’, fixed as a postposition: तेषां कृते ‘for their sake, on their account’.

mantras.anvaya: (एतत् किम्,) यत् चित्तं विगुणेषु अपि बन्धुषु प्रेमप्रवणम् (अस्ति), तेषां कृते मे निःश्वासः दौर्मनस्यं च जायते?
mantras.anvaya_en: A यत् clause (‘that …’) spelling out the एतत् of 1.32: two statements, the first nominal (verb ‘is’ understood), the second with जायते.
mantras.lit: — that the mind is inclined to love even toward worthless kinsfolk; that on their account sighing and dejection arise in me.
mantras.tr: — that my heart leans in love toward kinsfolk who have shown no virtue, and that I sigh and grieve for their sake.
mantras.tr_note: ‘my’ with heart is supplied from मे in the second line; the verse explains the ‘this’ (एतत्) of 1.32.

comm.t: The merchant names what he cannot understand: love that persists toward the unworthy, and the sighing and gloom it brings. The symptoms are bodily (निःश्वास) and mental (दौर्मनस्य).

A modern reading: the verse does not call the love wrong. It reports, without judgement, that love does not wait for its object to deserve it — which is both the merchant’s pain and, later in the text, the shape of the Goddess’s own compassion.

samasa.vigraha: न विद्यते प्रीतिः येषां ते, तेषु
samasa.literal: those for whom there is no love
samasa.alt: Also possible as a nañ tatpuruṣa noun, न प्रीतिः ‘absence of love’, in the locative plural: ‘amid (their) unkindnesses’. The bahuvrīhi fits better, since the word stands beside तेषु as its qualifier.

morph.note: Deliberative present, as in 1.31: करोमि किम् here answers किं करोमि there, so the merchant’s reply begins and ends with the same helpless question.
The adjective whose abstract noun (निष्ठुरता) appeared in 1.31; here neuter, agreeing with मनः.

mantras.anvaya: किं करोमि, यत् मनः तेषु अप्रीतिषु निष्ठुरं न (भवति)?
mantras.anvaya_en: A question with a causal यत् clause; the verb ‘is’ (भवति) is understood.
mantras.lit: What am I to do, since the mind is not hard toward those loveless ones?
mantras.tr: What am I to do? My heart will not harden against those who have no love for me.
mantras.tr_note: ‘for me’ makes explicit whom the kin do not love; the compound says only ‘without love’.

comm.t: The merchant closes his reply where he began (1.31): ‘What can I do?’ The repetition marks the end of his speech and of his own resources; the next step is to go to the sage.

sandhi.note: As in 1.1: the y that replaces the visarga before a vowel is dropped, and the vowels stand apart.

mantras.anvaya_en: Subject and verb: a speaker label.

comm.t: The frame narrator, Mārkaṇḍeya, speaking to his pupil Krauṣṭuki, takes up the story again: the conversation of the king and the merchant is over, and he tells how the two went together to the sage Medhas.
